utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Nicholls, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Actually, having gone through the transcript and discussing things, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, your Excellencies. Bear with me. I did not expect that I would be invited to do so immediately. Yes, a few short questions. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning everybody. Good morning Colonel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all let me ask you about the procedure to report crimes to the prosecutor's office? Who is it who reports crimes to the prosecutor's office, which structure in a unit?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to our rules as far as I can remember at this moment, but I believe that I will be right if I say that from the company commander down to every officer is duty-bound to draft a report and to hand it over to the prosecutor's office if they have a legal expert in their unit, i.e., in their command. It is that legal expert who drafts that report. Every officer who learns of a crime is duty-bound to examine it if possible, but he has to report it. It has to be done by a professional in that unit. Having done that, they have to report to their superiors about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the role of the military police in that?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any details. However, in that case the military police are used by the security organ of the command. I know approximately, but I don't want to go into detail of what the police need to do. In any case, it has -- the police have to follow the orders of the commander and investigate the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If the report has already reached the prosecutor's office, the prosecutor will be in charge -- in charge of the investigation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a telegram by Colonel Masal, and you saw how he interpreted the verbal words of General Mladic. Every ethnic community over there has some derogatory terms. How were we referred to by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are referred to as "vlasi."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many such terms which are customary, but they do not reflect the gist. It all depends on the objective which people want to achieve. In our documents issued by the organ for moral guidance, there are also elements of propaganda based on the truth. In other words, there are very few instances -- or, rather, it is not very realistic. It is somewhat coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are all Croats Ustasha for us or some are not?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Ustasha are only those who were soldiers in the Independent State of Croatia, i.e., in the state which was based and which arose from the traditions of the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the Turks, Skender Kulenovic, Mesa Selimovic, Osman Karabegovic, are they Turks?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who are Turks in colloquial terms?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In colloquial terms --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this refer to civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It refers to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there another even worse derogatory term which is used for Muslim civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're referring to the term "balija."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. I believe that some of the confusion arose with regard to the question as to whether the aerial bomb was launched from the ground or from the lorry. Did you make a distinction when you said that you didn't know whether it was from the ground or from the lorry?

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see where it was launched from and how. I never saw that launch. Therefore, I don't know where the launch is mounted, whether it is mounted on a lorry, on a platform, on the ground. In any case, it is not mounted on an aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, sir, this is all I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: LUKA DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Presiding Judge, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About what, Mr. Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, I would like to thank you for having intervened yesterday about the event in Gojcevic village. However, last night I had problems because I believe that it was not completely elucidated. Those were people who originated from that village and who left for Croatia before 1991 and since there was a census, they declared themselves as people who hailed from that village, but it is only certain that they left before 1991. In other words, the information about the number of people does not apply to the village of Gojcevic who lived there in 1993 and in 1994. And let me tell you that no single house was torched. There was no need to torch any houses over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, would you like to pose further questions with respect to comments he made right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Dragicevic on behalf of the Chamber I thank you for coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If I may, Excellencies, just while witness is outside, that is wrong with those censuses from Croatia. It says that inhabitants of Croatia originating from Bosnia. [Interpretation] I could have stated that in Serbian as well. The fact is that this creates confusion. There are original documents, there are original census documents in Bosnia, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. You can use that later on. Before -- yes. We'll bring in the next witness. In the meantime, I was informed by the Registry that the translation of Exhibit D2634 MFI has been uploaded, so I note that that would be admitted in full. The next witness is Mrs. Andjelkovic Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic, you will lead live this expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He was supposed to -- I was told that he was supposed to arrive at the Tribunal at quarter to 10.00. We will rise and then as soon as he arrives, if we could be informed accordingly. We'll rise. --- Break taken at 9.15 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, for the purpose of scheduling, you will take about an hour for your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I won't take more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break after the -- your examination-in-chief is over, and then we'll have the -- we'll hear the cross after the break. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you provide us with a copy of your CV?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D21079 in e-court. Could we have the English version as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly present your CV to us. First of all, tell us what your education is and what your profession is based on that training, what your doctorate was, what kind of work you did.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in technology and engineering. I graduated in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness will have to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, since your testimony is to be translated, if you could slow down a bit more and put a pause between the question and answer, and could you kindly repeat your answer, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it is: I graduated from high school, and then I graduated from the University of Belgrade. It was the Faculty of Technology and Metallurgy, and I got my Masters Degree at the department of organic chemistry, and I got my doctorate in the field of explosives. I worked at the military technical institute from 1974 until 1989. That's when I got my Masters Degree. And then from the Military Technical Institute I went to work in another research institute. In the military technical institute I was involved in studying new explosives and new technologies, the processing of explosives, then their elaboration into weaponry and explosives, TNT, and studying their characteristics. So this was research based on knowledge about explosives. Then I went in 1989 to work up until 2000 when I retired in the technical experimental centre. Over there I worked on the verification and testing of various weapons containing explosives. At the technical experimental centre I received my doctorate. For many years I was a member of the scientific council and I continued my research work. I wrote several monographs in the field of explosives, and also quite a few professional publications that I presented in my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that it doesn't say here in line 4 that this scientific council was also the scientific and teaching council. Can you tell us what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not a technical and teaching -- or, rather, it is not research and teaching. If it were the VMA, which is also a teaching institution, that would have been different, but I was member of the scientific council of the centre and before that also at the VTI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did this have to do with practical questions of applying your knowledge concerning weapons? How was this used in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Members of the scientific council were - how shall I put this? - eminent scholars from these institutions, and for the most part they based their work on the development of new scientific methods and also developed various resources. Also, they were mentors for people who were getting their masters and doctoral degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This component experimental, did that have any kind of concrete -- concrete effect on the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: This experimental or testing institute was a pre-eminent institution for testing weapons. All new equipment that was supposed to be commissioned in the JNA had to go through this channel. Not a single piece of equipment could be used in the JNA unless it had been seriously and extensively tested at the Technical Testing Centre. Now, what does this involve? Technical documentation, construction documentation, all standards that have to do with each and every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, could I just ask you, please, to speak a bit slower, because we would really like to have each and every word of yours recorded in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was done finally? You say that no piece of equipment could be -- well, what did this imply?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Once a piece of equipment is tested very extensively, then a special licence is issued -- or, rather, a special document introducing this piece of equipment into the weaponry of the JNA at the time. Without this kind of extensive testing for all components of each and every piece of equipment, no piece of equipment could have been included in the JNA weaponry; that is to say, the weapons they had available to them, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How was this reflected on the possibility of manufacturing this?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as manufacturing is concerned, there was the military industry, product specific as it was called. It was highly developed in the then SFRY. It had units that co-operated with the military technical institute and -- and they co-operated with the military technical institute and developed certain assets regardless of whether it's ammunition or vehicles. Then before they would test a particular piece at the Technical Testing Centre, they had their own facilities where they would test a particular piece of equipment, and once they had done that, then it would be brought to the centre where preliminary testing would be conducted, and then it would be checked. If everything was all right, then it could be studied in its final stage. So this was a rather serious procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the international reputation of the Yugoslav military industry at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The military industry of the SFRY was among the best in the world. It was a renowned institution, and I think that it ranked fifth among weapon exporters in the world, especially artillery, ammunition, vehicles, tanks, the M-84 tank, for instance, that was the crown, if you will, of the then military industry of the SFRY. So it enjoyed quite a reputation both in Europe and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this CV? Can it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D2661.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic, can you tell us what the Defence team asked you to do for the Defence, what kind of research?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The Defence team asked me a while ago to carry out, of course in co-operation with my colleagues, a review and analysis of two reports of my colleague Berko Zecevic that pertained to the use of bombs in urban areas in Sarajevo. One of these reports is from 1995, and the other one is from 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up 1D6820 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your report Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was anything redacted here? All right. Sorry. Sorry. We did that. Actually, we redacted things that were not contained in the indictment against me because they were unnecessary. However, the indictment was amended several times, and that's why all of this happened. Can I ask you whether it is correct that Mr. Zecevic, in his findings, presented the following thesis: That classical explosive charges of air-bombs that the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska had and that were Yugoslav made, that these classical charges were replaced by the so-called RAE explosive, and could you tell us in simple terms what this report of his contained, the one that is being challenged by the Defence, and then I will put some specific questions regarding these differences.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The thesis of my colleague Zecevic was that air-bombs were used. I'm sorry, I seem to have lost the thread.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How were they manufactured, these bombs, or, rather, how were these explosive charges changed?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Ah, all right. First of all, as far as air-bombs were concerned, those that already existed in the weaponry of the JNA, TNT was used as a charge, and that is how they were manufactured, filled with TNT. It was physically impossible to replace this TNT and to put air explosives in there quite simply because these casings of air-bombs are much thicker than the casings of containers that contain air explosives. So it is quite impossible that warheads could be an aerosol explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I just wanted to ask you something. What was supposed to be done to a bomb, what was supposed to be modified on the bomb, on the warhead itself, in order to replace this?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the assumption is -- the assumption is, but it is highly unlikely, to get the explosive out, to melt it, if you will, and then when this warhead or casing is cleaned in this way, if you will, then you put ethylene oxide inside. That's the aerosol explosive that is most often referred to. And then in the middle a cylinder called charge should be put in with classical explosives, say 10 to 15 per cent of the mass of the overall explosive. And then there would be a detonation of this middle charge which would open the warhead, and then this aerosol would be released. And that is absolutely impossible in the case of casings of warheads of air-bombs because they are so thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I see a sketch somewhere in your report of what you described to us just now, and can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I get my paper out of my bag now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that the Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please assist the Registry and tell us the page where that can be found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an image, image 29. Image 29. In my report it is on page 57, and in Mr. Zecevic's report it is -- do I have to provide you with that page as well or is it enough if you have my page? But I think that the -- there is a discrepancy of one or two pages in respect of my report. In any case, it's image 29.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was this: Here we can see a charge. What charge is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The -- based on the particles that were found belonging to an air-bomb, Mr. Zecevic here drew an image of a rocket projectile with a warhead, and he assumes that the charge was aerosol explosive. The warhead depicted in this way is a warhead which corresponds to the casing of an air-bomb. So this cannot be a container filled with liquid explosive because there is a thickening at the top, as you can see. There is a thickening at the bottom, and on average the thickness of a casing in bombs is about 10 millimetres in the narrowest part and then towards the top this increases by two or even by three times. I don't know much about that but I know that the increase in the thickness is significant at the top as well as at the bottom. In the middle what you see as a darker part is a classical explosive charge. What is the function of that classical explosive? The function is as follows: The middle part of the classical explosive at any given moment when a bomb comes to -- to a certain distance, there's a special way of functioning of that bomb. It does not function as an aircraft bomb that is thrown and detonated. This is a bomb which has special demands in terms of altitude. It has certain measuring devices which determine the height and the distance of the bomb from the ground which is 5 to 10 metres depending on the target. And then the inner part explodes, that inner part, and the explosion is aimed at breaking up the container which contains the aerosol explosives. And when that container is broken, then the aerosol explosive which is liquid at 0 degrees centigrade and at 20 degrees is a gas, that becomes a cloud, and then there's a special detonator which initiates the explosion, enters the cloud and it initiates the explosion. The size of that cloud is about 20 to -- 15 to 20 metres in diametre. The pressure in that cloud according to literature is about 20 to 30 bars, and I calculated based on the speed of the detonation of 1500 to 20 or even 3000 metres in a second. My calculations say that the pressure in that cloud is between 5 and 20 bars. I have to say here that according to literature, referring to explosives and their action, and which is something that I learned in my profession, and I noticed it very well, are not always in correlation with the experiment. They are always higher. I really don't know why.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know when I dealt with my explosives and when I examined the speed of detonation, when I had all the conditions that were present in literature --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down. The witness is speaking very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the speed of detonation, so I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you slow down again. It's very difficult for the interpreters to keep up with you, in particular we are dealing with such expert matters. Shall we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We did not miss anything, but we kindly ask the witness to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you start again from the speed of detonation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll try and slow down. When that cloud spreads, a special initiator of the explosion enters the cloud and initiates the explosion in the cloud, which means what we get is an explosive cloud. The speed of detonation of that cloud, i.e., the speed by which the chemical reaction spreads through that cloud is between 1500 and 3000 metres per second, and the pressure of the detonation is between 20 to 30 bars. However, when I calculated based on the thickness of the ethylene oxide which was 89 at 20 degrees, and based on the speed of the detonation according to literature, I obtained a pressure of detonation ranging between 5 and 20 bars, i.e., the median pressure of 11 bars. I must intervene at this point, and I must say that what we find in literature is never in correlation with what we obtain in experimental situations, and I know that very well from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I would like to ask you this: How would it be possible to empty the casing from TNT and replace the content by partially hard and partially liquid explosives as is represented in here?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Air-bombs contain liquid trotyl. That trotyl melts at 82 degrees. Thus melted, it can be transported into the casing of a warhead and then its manufacture is finished. In order to pour out, i.e., to melt that trotyl from the warhead which weighs between 100 and 250 kilogrammes and which contains between 39 to 105 melted trotyl, requires a lot of work and effort. That warhead has to be lifted to an elevated position, the lower part has to be unscrewed, and water steam which has to be heated up to 90 degrees centigrade, the trotyl has to be melted layer by layer. It has to be collected in a container and then it has to be removed. It is a very painstaking job which doesn't pay at the end. It is pointless at the end of the day. And then those empty casings are filled with containers with aerosol explosives. Again, this doesn't make too much sense because I've just told you -- I've just explained to you the techniques of the casing of an air-bomb in -- on average -- on average is about 10 millimetres, which means that in -- that the central charge which is in the middle of liquid explosive would not have enough power and strength to break up that casing in the first place, because the container in which liquid explosive is placed, its thickness is about 2 to 3 millimetres, and that's a big difference in terms of the casing of the warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a certain height. What did you mean when you say that at a certain height this aerosol bomb will explode? How does that reflect on the point of contact with the soil?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Aerosol bombs are primarily constructed to make passages through jungles, for example. When the Americans first arrived in Vietnam and Cambodia, they did that. The principle of action of this air-bomb is as follows: An aircraft drops an aircraft bomb at a certain level or a certain height. A parachute opens. Those are such manipulations to allow the aircraft to get away from the bomb as quickly as possible. A parachute thus opens, and at the same time the altitude metre switches itself on, and after a certain time that determines at which height or at which level the central charge will be detonated. That bomb usually comes 5 to 10 metres away from the target, and it all depends on what the target is, whether it s a bunker or making a road through a minefield and so on and so forth. When that bomb opens after the central charge explodes and when the container opens and bigger fragments of tin start falling out, then from special places on the warhead which sometimes can be a tail fin near the parachute, the fuses ignite a fire in the cloud, and that cloud falls onto the ground and with its pressure it prompts certain actions. This is primarily made to destroy personnel, to destroy bunkers, and that bomb is made in such a way to leave larger facilities intact, but at the same time it destroys the enemy forces in the pockets around those facilities such as bunkers and trenches and so on and so forth. There is no way to save yourselves from that cloud. When it falls on the ground, all the living beings are damaged by that cloud. They can suffer major injuries from that cloud, which means that its lethal properties are active in three-quarters of its diametre. Usually the casualties are affected by the blast effect. The temperatures are high, up to 3.000 degrees centigrade, and injuries consist of burns and similar injuries. And if the impact area is near a building, you can see charred windows and doors. Unfortunately, I had an opportunity to be an expert witness for explosions from methane which is also an aerosol that is used as a charge for such bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we deal with the effects, I wanted to ask you whether the ratio between the charge and the thickness of the casing, does it also influence the fragmentation of the casing?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course. One always has to be borne -- take into account that there is about 30 to 40 per cent of the explosive with respect to the weight of the casing. In aircraft bombs the situation is the same. For example, when the weight is 100 kilogrammes, there is 39 kilogrammes of explosive. So the ratio is some -- between 30 to 40 per cent. I get carried away. 30 or 40 per cent of explosive with respect to the weight of the casing. What happens with the destructive bombs? When the secondary explosive explodes in the casing, i.e., when trotyl explosive explodes, the casing is fragmented due to the chemical reaction which happens in the explosive when it is initiated. That means that the explosive is initiated when it receives a heat impulse from the primary explosive, from the propellant. A very quick chemical reaction develops. It advances through the explosive and releases a high quantity of warmth, and warm, hot gases are developed under pressure. They destroy the metal body, and they have a destructive effect when -- and that casing also has a lethal effect due its fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us with this: It seems to me on the basis of your remarks so far that the explosion of liquid explosives happens only after fragmentation -- or, rather, the breaking of the container. Does the liquid explosive take part in fragmentation or does this happen after -- after, you know, what you said, when the liquid gas got out?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the basic difference in terms of how these classical explosives function and these liquid explosives is as follows: Trotyl, now I'm speaking about that, has sufficient energy in it, its molecules have sufficient energy, so it can react on land, in air. It doesn't need oxygen. It reacts within the casing and fragments the casing. This air-bomb consists of compounds that have one or two atoms of oxygen, C2H4O specifically in this case, that's the structural formula. It doesn't have enough oxygen; therefore, it cannot burn. When the container is opened, I mean as far as fuel-air explosives are concerned, the role of the casing is not the same as in cases of classical bombs, that is to say including fragmentation. Here the casing is used only as clothing, if you will, for liquid explosive, and then when it is opened, then this liquid explosive has to be triggered off in some way in order to take oxygen from the air and then start burning. So that's the difference. Solid explosives do not need oxygen. This is an adiabatic process, but the case of liquid explosives, that is not the case. There has to be oxygen for it to react. Those are the basic differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me help the interpreters. And you can help, too. Adiabatic, line 5, would you translate it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: That's what we said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is a situation when there is no exchange of energy with the environment. The change occurs within the body itself without the participation of the external environment. That is an adiabatic process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what happens if the quantity of explosive that is supposed to fragment a casing is smaller than necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: This container with the liquid explosive; right? Well, nothing can happen. I mean, well, if it is less than what is prescribed, there cannot be fragmentation. There's simply not enough strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across any information to the effect that the Army of Republika Srpska was technically and technologically capable of replacing these two explosives, replacing TNT with this liquid explosive?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Something like that did exist in the SFRY, in the JNA, only in one particular overall institution. It was an institute in Tivat. It was called Sava Kovacevic, and nowhere else. Otherwise, it would have been very, very risky to embark on any such thing. They had all the necessary technical equipment for doing something like that. Otherwise, I did not know of any capability of the army of the Republika Srpska to do something like that. That is a very painstaking job, and ultimately it is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that it doesn't really pay off, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant energy consumption. Also, if there is a proper piece of ammunition, why would one make something different with a very uncertain outcome? I mean, what would be the point of all of that? I don't see the actual point of something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Yugoslavia, either the SFRY or in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were air-bombs fully researched, and were they ever introduced as a standard weapon of the JNA or, rather, the VJ? Aerosol, I mean. Oh, it said here air-bomb, whereas I said aerosol.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I spent my entire career working with explosives and during the second part of my career I also tested quality, I can say with a high degree of responsibility that something like that never reached my desk. Why? At the Technical Testing Centre I was the only expert for explosives. As I said a moment ago, in order for a piece of equipment to be admitted into the JNA, it had to go through all the necessary testing starting with documentation, construction and technical documentation. That is to see how the piece was constructed, what the standards involved were. Each and every expert had their own fields. I covered the field of explosives. So everything that had to do with explosives had to reach my desk. It could go no further until I initialed it. During my career until the year 2000, I did not receive any such thing at my desk, and I can say with full responsibility that something like that did not exist in the weaponry of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 18 did you say that you were the only expert?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said I was the only expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the consequences would be shown by a pathology or postmortem on a living creature who would fall victim to one of these explosives and if you would compare that to someone who would be a victim of another explosive rather than the one we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm a layperson, but I think I can describe that. Destructive bombs, lethal weapons with thick casings, have a lethal -- or, rather, a destructive effect and are lethal as far as personnel are concerned. That is shrapnel, different open wounds and so on. Everything that can be assumed what can happen to a human being when hit by a metal object that is moving at such high speed. On the other hand, as far as aerosol explosives are concerned, or fuel-air explosives, primarily they have a blast effect on human beings more than is the case in the former. So there are injuries sustained by internal organs, the brain, ears, lungs, heart. The lungs and heart can stop altogether. Air can penetrate veins and so on. So wounds from fuel-air explosives are usually due to a blast effect. Also, there can be burns, because this cloud is very hot, 2000 to 3000 degrees. So in my view, one of the dominant effects of this cloud are actually burns, and I had occasion to see that when I was an expert witness with regards to such explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, thank you. Can we just explain this, transcript page 22, line 11. It says that you're a layperson. What is it that you're a layperson for?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Layperson as far as wounds are concerned. I'm not a physician. So when I talk about wounds, injuries, I am saying that as a layperson. I'm not a doctor. I'm not a physician. That's how I meant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Secondly, you mentioned eyes and the transcript does not reflect eyes. What happens with eyes in case of these two explosives?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as these classical explosives are concerned, the wounds are as if they were inflicted by a bullet, let me put it that way. And as far as these liquid explosives are concerned, these wounds are due to pressure. That is to say that there is pressure. The eyes can fall out of the sockets. Then there can be -- then lungs can also be injured. I mean, all of these are the effects of the blast effect. Because the pressure in that cloud is -- well, 50 to 20 bar, and literature says 20 to 30 bar, but I just did the calculation now. All right. This pressure, when compared to the pressure when a -- when classical ammunition explodes, classical TNT explosives, it's much less. When trotyl explodes, it is 200 kilobar. Imagine 200 times 10 to the third. So the pressure of fuel-air explosives is up to 20 bar. But this goes on a bit longer, this pressure, a few milliseconds. When compared to the pressure from classical explosives, that is much shorter. And that is what I have to say about the blast effect of these fuel-air explosives. Perhaps it's more pronounced than as far as classical explosives are concerned, although it does exist there as well but if they are closer to the centre of explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do these explosives behave in relation to physical solid obstacles or, rather, shelters, if a human being, a living creature were to be behind something like that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The diametre of their clouds is from 17 to 20 metres. My colleague mentions the diametre of even 30 metres. There is no shelter there for human beings, none whatsoever. Why? Because this explosive -- this explosive cloud, this cloud that exploded if I can put it that way, penetrates everywhere. If in one area there is a cloud and if it detonates, then no one can be saved from that. You cannot stand behind a pillar, for instance, because it sinks everything like a fluid or liquid does, whereas in the case of classical explosives, a shelter can be found from the blast. You can stand behind a pillar, behind some kind of concrete shelter, and then the blast can just pass -- or, rather, bypass that obstacle. And then if a man is sheltered or is hiding there can remain unharmed. Things like that have happened. That's the difference between the two blast effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity of seeing for yourself and recording any kind of pathology findings or postmortems or descriptions of a site where such an explosion took place involving high temperatures, what the effects were on the environment and also were there pathology findings for human beings or other living creatures that would confirm that this fuel-air explosive had been used in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to start by dealing with physical remains of an explosion. The primary thing is when a container with fuel-air explosive explodes, large parts of the metal casing are separated, 300 by 400 millimetres. That is to say it's like pieces of tin that would be on site. That was not found anywhere. This was not even reviewed theoretically in the reports that I looked at, the fragmentation of a casing with fuel-air explosive. Nowhere in these materials did I observe that in addition to destruction effects were shown of burning, combustion. These are dominant effects in addition to destruction, in addition to the blast effect. There's also burning. I didn't see that anywhere. As far as these post-mortems are concerned, I did not have an opportunity of seeing that anywhere. I didn't see any burns, any cases of burns. I saw two or three cases. I didn't see more. But there was no reference to any person who had been wounded or killed had suffered burns, and that would have to happen if there was a burning cloud, if I can put it in such picturesque terms. That is what this explosion is called when that kind of explosive explodes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Did you correct anything, or did you amend your basic findings?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I added something. I sent that addition to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I like to call up 1D6816 in e-court. And I will tender both documents after we have finished with them. 1D6816.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have that. It has three pages, and I have them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can this errata be replaced by the word "addendum"? The title is "Errata." Did you correct anything or did you add anything?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: In my copy the title is an addition to the expert analysis. I don't know how this was admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was translated as "errata."

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's okay. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what your addition was?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see in figure 1 that my colleague in his report that he drafted in 2007, on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which colleague is that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berko Zecevic, my colleague who drafted a report in 2007, on page 06067086 showed a photo in his report - it's image 99, and in my addendum it's image 1 - and he described the differences, and he also had some footnotes about the remains of the propellant of the modified bomb FAB-250 found when the building in Dositejeva Street was targeted. He doesn't mention the number of that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To help the participants in the proceedings, the reference is 1D6838, page 73 in e-court. That's the reference for the expert's words, and that's the Serbian version. And the doctor provided the ERN page. Page 73 in the Serbian version, 1D6838.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Doctor. Please continue. I just wanted the participants to be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The rocket engines in my figure 1 is something that Berko Zecevic found in Dositejeva Street according to him. Figure two depicts the same object from a different angle and that was found in Geteova 5 or Cetinjska 5 in Sarajevo. On the following page of my supplement figure 3 depicts the remains of the engine that was found in Dositejeva Street number 4A. What we see in figure 3 and in figure 1, those things do not resemble each other at all. In my expert report, what you see under figure 3 are the remains of rocket engines in Dositejeva Street. In -- this is what is found in Berko Zecevic's report, and this is how the engines look when they're separated, whereas in figure 1 he put them together, and they resemble -- not only do they resemble, but they are the same engines that are found in figure 2, and that is what exists in the 1995 report that concerns Geteova Street. Furthermore, on the following page is a figure from his document, figure 99, and you can see footnote 8, the remains of the propellant of the modified bomb found when a building in Dositejeva Street was targeted. And below that you can see the racketised [phoen] bomb, FAB-250. The photos were taken by the Dutch unit of the SFOR where you can see the warhead FAB-250, and my colleague Zecevic in his report expressly claimed that it was charged with fuel-air explosive and not only FAB-250 but also FAB-100 which you can see in my report here, and he says in his report that it is a pity that one could not find a single bomb that could be de-elaborated or deconstructed in order to identify the explosive within. And in his reports -- in both of his reports, in several places he shows the FAB-100 bomb which was found as an unexploded, and now the FAB-250 bomb which also was not activated, and my question to my esteemed colleague Berko Zecevic is this: How come the warheads of those rockets that were found were not reconstructed in order to establish or to refute the opinion that it contained fuel-air explosives?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about modified air-bombs, is something really modified on the bomb itself?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: In this case that we considered here, the only thing that was modified was the propellant. The bomb was not thrown from an aircraft, but, rather, something was mounted to that bomb, certain motors or engines which propelled it to the place where it was supposed to explode, and that was the modification that was made. Those modifications did not constitute the replacement of a solid explosive by fuel-air explosive. At least based on the findings that I analysed here. I didn't find any such thing, nothing to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 69, i.e., on Mr. Zecevic's report page, can you look at the words ODAB and KREMA in the right-hand side part of the photo.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous page, please. Is this it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a comparison between the FAB-250 and ODAB-500 and in the photo itself it says, "KREMA the rocket rear view"?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: You know what? Despite my best intentions, despite all of my efforts, as I was reading his report I could not understand what my colleague, Berko Zecevic, understood when he used the term "KERMA." I understand the ODAB-500, it's a Russian air-bomb which is thrown from an aircraft and just a while ago we saw its image, but when it comes to KREMA I really could not understand what he was talking about. I don't know because that word does not ring a bell. I don't know what he meant when he used the term "KREMA." There was a hint to the Russian-made bomb, the Russian KREMA. I really did not understand from his report what he was alluding to, and I even put that as part of my report, that his explanation of KREMA really didn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one word, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic. In his report, did Dr. Zecevic provide any evidence that fuel-air bombs were used during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on my research and examination of those two reports, I did not find anything that would have been typical of an explosion of fuel-air explosives. In other words, in his reports, he did not describe even the fragments of such a destructive bomb. He stated that there were no fragments, and based on that he concluded that all the bombs were fuel-air bombs. My colleague Zecevic's claims that those were fuel-air bombs was based on the absence of fragments. However, if the fuel-air bombs had been used, one would have had to find at least a few larger fragments of containers, because those are light particles whose speed is not very high because the fuel-air explosive does not have such a high speed in order to be able to propel those particles very far. So the particles of that container if fuel-air explosives had been used should have had to have been found. Absolutely they would have had to have been found. On the other hand, in the facilities where FAB destructive bombs were used, in addition to the destruction effects which should not have had been so large as I saw them, one would have also had to have noticed some charred remains of wooden surfaces such as furniture and doors and windows to show that there was flame, because flame is one of the dominant features of fuel-air explosives. I claim that with full responsibility because I had occasions to see the effects of explosions of natural gas in residential homes which has the same destructive effect as fuel-air explosives. So -- another thing, burns were not noticed on people who were injured. No big tin particles were found, and they should have been. And that is my conclusion. Based on those very significant pieces of evidence, I can say that fuel-air bombs were not used in Sarajevo. And he confirms that himself in a written form in one part of his written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, where do we see the word "KREMA" in Mr. Zecevic's report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, on the left side of the screen, the bottom right photo it says on the photo itself, "KREMA-4, rocket rear view."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more question, madam. We see the term ODAB-500 here. What is the weight of that Russian-made air-bomb?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: They weigh over 500 kilos, and together with -- actually, their mass is 520 kilogrammes, and the charge weighs about 200 kilos of fuel-air explosive. The thickness of their casing is up to 3 millimetres. The casings are thin. Therefore, they are thrown from an aircraft. They have a parachute, and they have everything that I already described, altitude metre, the secondary fuse that are activated within the cloud and detonate it. But they are much bigger, of a bigger size, and they are much, much more destructive and lethal. That asset is rather lethal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That weight, would it require a somewhat different propellant if it was not thrown from an aircraft but, rather, launched from a launcher?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I never reflected on that. Its weight is much too big to be launched from a launcher. Under bullet point 9, Mr. Zecevic in one place says that its weight without fuel is 706 kilogrammes, and in another place it says that ODAB-500 weighs about 250 kilos. You see, he frequently changes the characteristics of that bomb. At places it's 706 without fuel and in other places 520. However, be it as it may, it's a very heavy bomb, and if you were to add engines or motors to it, it would weigh even more, and I don't know what kind of a launcher it should -- should it be to launch it. Those would have to be very special launchers that would be able to carry such a huge weight. I believe that it could not be launched from the ground, although -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender the redacted report, the redacted expert report by Dr. Mirjana Andjelkovic Lukic which is 1D6820 here, as well as its supplement which is 1D6816.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report should be assigned Exhibit D2662, and the corrigenda shall be assigned Exhibit D2663. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic, you told us earlier that you worked at the Technical Testing Centre from around 1989 until 2000 or was it 2002?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Until 2000. I was retired in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your CV says 2002, but I'll take 2000. So during those 11 years --

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let me see. Just a moment, I need to see. Maybe it was a slip. Yes. I'm sorry. Until 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during those 13 years you were undoubtedly involved in the testing of many different kinds of weapon systems and many different kinds of munitions.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And in your evidence today, you -- as you put it, not a single piece of equipment could be used in the JNA unless it had been seriously and extensively tested at the Technical Testing Centre.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your evidence earlier, you described some of the steps of the testing process, and in your report you also refer to other steps. You refer to prototype, you prefer to test production run, you refer to testing of batches for consistency. Could you help me understand the process of testing of any new weapon system from the moment when an initial blueprint is produced until it is approved for service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. First of all, the time of development from the idea to develop this idea until it is developed takes seven to eight years. That's an optimal amount of time during which you make all the documentation, test all the materials, and there are a lot of steps in between until you make an initial sample that needs to be tested on the testing ground of the factory itself. They have such testing grounds also, but they also use the grounds of the Technical Testing Centre if they don't have their own for such an asset. So the factory that produces the asset registers them first as sample pieces. That is usually 10 to 20 samples. It could be more if it's profitable for them, but it's not often the case, because the production is very expensive and you try to be as rational as possible. Those are sample pieces on which testing is done. The testing is for efficiency and for their fitness to technical requirements. That means effect on the target, how it acts on the target, it be an ammunition or another type of weapon. Now I'm talking about explosives. Whether the explosive is well placed in the asset, whether it gives good results in terms of penetration, et cetera. When you finish the testing with sample pieces and the documentations, because it's not only the asset itself, it's a huge amount of documentation documenting the construction. For instance, if it's an artillery round or a bomb or a cumulative article with optimal penetrating force, all this has a complete documentation, and for every document in that set you have a standard. If it's about steel, then what kind of steel. If it's tested. If it's an explosive, what type of explosive. What its characteristics are, pyrotechnics of it, anti-corrosion protection, so all the elements that can affect the efficiency and the life of this asset. All that is recorded in the technical documentation. We even have a standard for paints. It has to be anti-corrosive. It must not produce any effects when exposed to light, et cetera. It goes into the greatest detail. Then later when you check all that, when the experts from the Technical Testing Centre see that this construction and technical documentation is all right, that the asset produced on the testing ground, the effects that have been envisaged, then we can think about multi-series -- sorry, zero series. After the testing follows the zero series, which means that the production has been mastered, the asset goes to the factory and is definitively produced there. After that, it goes back for testing to the Technical Testing Centre so that if certain shortcomings have been noticed on the sample pieces, and that usually happens, we have to see whether these shortcomings have been redressed and removed, and if that is the case, we proceed with the zero series and make a final assessment. It happens that an asset is rejected because it is not good or it needs to be improved. That means that it did not produce the desired required effects. However, usually it is approved, and when the zero series is approved, then it goes into production. That is the usual lengthy process.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I help with the transcript? On this page 35, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic said Pala series, and then she said that the time for development is five to seven years, whereas the record says seven to eight years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five to seven years, yes, yes. It takes five to seven years. That means a total number of seven years or a total number of eight -- seven years.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pala series" should be "failed series."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please confirm the name of the first series. We heard it as zero series. We don't understand the Pala series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will you take that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic, you referred to in your evidence zero series; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic, this entire process that you've described, does that take place prior to a phase of test firing of the weapon system in order to create firing tables?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as the firing tables are concerned, I told you that I've never done that. I've never even come close. The only thing I can tell you is that sample pieces precede the zero series. The zero series is the one that confirms that the asset has met all the requirements, tactical and technical requirements, and also in terms of construction and technical documentation. As for the rest, it is understood that all that is all right, and if you say firing tables, I have never dealt with that. I am an expert in explosives. I only looked at the effect on explosives in the asset in which it is placed, whether it functions in the way that I expected it to from the construction documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now during your service at the JNA Military Technical Institute between 1974 and 1989 and your further 13 years at the Technical Testing Centre, you unquestionably became aware of the concept of firing tables; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: That is something that my colleagues in artillery and ballistics do. I have nothing to do with it. Of course I know they exist and they are necessary, indispensable, but I really have nothing to do with it. I deal exclusively with explosives. I'm somebody who worked to study explosives and their characteristics and monitored how those explosives act when fired on a plate on the testing ground or when fired from an artillery weapon, but I know nothing about these firing tables. That's not what I'm expert in. I'm a technologist, a chemical engineer. I didn't even have that as a subject at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You'll nevertheless accept on the basis of your very extensive experience in the JNA that new munitions and new weapon systems were subjected to hundreds and in many cases thousands of test firings in order to create comprehensive and reliable firing tables?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you this again: As far as firing tables are concerned, I cannot provide you with any information because I don't know even approximately how many times something needs to be fired. I'm not a ballistics person, but I know when you test an asset, we always try to do it in the most economical way as far as my line of work is concerned, because testing is expensive. We try -- in fact, we tried to spend as little money and resources to get as accurate results as possible, but I really don't know anything about ballistics, and I cannot tell you anything that could be relevant to this trial. I'm really, really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I think you confirmed in your evidence in chief, but it's right, isn't it, that a new weapon system would not be deployed by the JNA without going through this comprehensive testing system as well as test firings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing. When you test a large system like a new artillery weapon or a vehicle, a whole team of people is engaged in it. We experts are little cogs in the wheel. I for instance am one who contributes to the process, but overall speaking, there is one main person surrounded by a team who manages the whole system. And of course not a single asset was included in the arsenal before passing through very comprehensive research and testing. At least while I worked in the Technical Testing Centre that never happened. I don't know what the situation is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move to the subject now of air-bombs generally speaking. You're familiar with the FAB-100 and the FAB-250?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'll just quickly go through a few matters that I think we can agree on. First of all, they were both unguided air-bombs, that is, there was no GPS or laser or any other kind of guidance system?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Those bombs are unguided air-bomb like modern air-bombs which can have GPS, laser guidance, and other guidance, remote guidance, but I believe in most armies today there exist those unguided bombs that are launched, dropped by an aircraft on a target; such are FAB-100 and FAB-250, they are unguided air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 14 should read "unlike modern bombs," not "like modern bombs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic, we can agree, I think, that both the FAB-100 and FAB-250 are designed to be dropped from the aircraft and to strike the ground at a near vertical angle?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's how they were designed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the casings of these bombs can be made of different metals with different densities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: No, because those casings of bombs have a precisely prescribed composition, because they had passed through certain testing that I talked to you about earlier, and they have a specified type of steel which I cannot name now, but it's all clearly written in the documentation. It cannot be just any old metal. It has to have certain solidity and specified percentages of steel and carbon and all the other additives, and it has to have prescribed sturdiness. You cannot put into that composition whatever you like. There is a specified composition and that's it. There are no deviations. So that they have clearly defined composition of metal that has to be a constant. It's prescribed and specified. There can be no departure from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we agree that the FAB-250 comes in more than one variety? For example, the FAB-250 M-72 contains 96 kilogrammes of TNT, and the FAB-250 M-79 contains 105 kilogrammes of TNT.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them is an older modification with less explosives, 97, and the other one has 105 kilos of explosive. That's FAB-250. That's a later generation, and you are correct, it's 105 kilogrammes of TNT.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the Military Technical Institute in Belgrade, did you occasionally test and approval air-bombs for use?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: The testing of air-bombs was finished in that year when they were nominated in 1979 and 1972, and that was finished then and it's no longer tested. Let me tell you why, because every factory -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We're under a little bit of time pressure so I'd just like to carry on if I can. Could you just tell us briefly, would a FAB-100 or FAB-250 air-bomb, generally speaking, be intended for dropping onto a predominantly civilian urban area?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: You know if that is your intention -- what do you mean dropping it on an urban area?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What I mean is are they approved for use for dropping from an aircraft onto a predominantly civilian urban area?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: These bombs fall under destructive bombs and they are designed for easily determined targets. That means bunkers, fortifications, for creating a passage, perhaps, for certain military targets. So that these bombs have exclusively the nature of being designed for destroying enemy fortified facilities. Not in terms of underground warehouses but surface fortifications like depots storing certain equipment or bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to the subject of modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 9, it's not "easily determined," but "easily fortified" or "lightly fortified." I do not -- I believe that the better translation would be "lightly fortified."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are pretty sure that we've heard correctly the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The word was "lako utvrdjeni." I don't think the translation is correct. The problem is that this word may mean both "determined" and "fortified" in our language. The verb "utvrdjeni" means "to determine," but it also means "to fortify."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, do you follow? Did you say that the -- these bombs were designed for easily determined targets, or could you clarify what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I say it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Easy to note targets or lightly fortified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I answer? Am I to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are very well military fortified targets such as underground depots that you cannot destroy with one bomb. You cannot even damage them with one bomb. But there are other surface fortifications that can be neutralised by such bombs. So the latter depots, to put it in military terms, are more lightly fortified. But these are depots that have a certain strength. They are not built like residential buildings, but they have a certain sturdiness because they house military equipment. So we can call them lightly fortified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on, as I said, to the subject of modified air-bombs. From your report and from the report which you contributed to along with Mrs. Subotic and Mr. Poparic concerning modified air-bombs, and from the report that you contributed to along with Mrs. Subotic and Mr. Poparic concerning the evidence of Berko Zecevic and Richard Higgs, I think we can agree in 1994 and 1995 the VRS fired modified FAB-100 and FAB-250 air-bombs at the very least into the city of Sarajevo using ground launched rockets that were attached to those air-bombs?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: In my report I did not contest that. Of course, these things existed and you can see that from the report. However, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think I'll move on. You also do not contest that these weapon systems existed in different configurations. For example, there was the FAB-100 with one rocket motor or three rocket motors. There was the FAB-250 with different numbers of rocket motors.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. FAB-100 was mainly with one rocket motor, but they could occur with three motors which is in my report, and you can see it in Mr. Berko's report, and it was with three rocket motors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And these different systems have different weights and different propulsive forces, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: As for explosive force, it is contained in the bombs, in FAB-100 and FAB-250. That is, its explosive force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And my point was that the propulsive force is different. Obviously if its being propelled by three rockets, the propulsive force would be different than if it was propelled by two rockets or one rocket. I'm sure we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: You know what? According to some technical logic I could agree with you, but I cannot say anything more about that to you because this is really not my field. I'm not a ballistics person. I mean, there is a technical logic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to go back to your periods working in the testing and approval of munitions. If you were asked to approve for use an unguided air-bomb to be propelled in a rocket-assisted configuration, you would expect that kind of system to be thoroughly and extensively tested before being approved for use?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: My role was not to deal with the entire system. I explained to you a moment ago that there were these so-called system engineers who were in charge of the system. They were the ones who decided whether they would apply this in this way or that way. My task was only to see whether the explosive in the asset had certain irregularities that could lead to an undesirable explosion or to some kind of excessive thing so that people who operate these pieces might fall victim in some way. I wanted to see whether the trotyl was properly charged, whether there were any voids. Sometimes I even had to X-ray all of this to see whether everything was done properly. So really, I cannot give you the kind of answer that I would like to give you from the point of view of a scientist, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, do you accept that if an institution as sophisticated as the Military Technical Institute in Belgrade were to be presented with a new weapon system such as a modified air-bomb where that weapon system came in different varieties with different weights, different numbers of rockets, different types of rockets, the proper thing to do would be to rigorously test each and every one of those variations, including hundreds of test firings, before it could be approved for use?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: When I spoke previously, I said -- I explained this to you, what the procedure was when studying a particular piece of equipment. This procedure does not differ greatly from one asset to another. If it was an expensive asset, efforts were made not to squander any money, because all of this does cost money. So when these systems were being tested - how do I put this? - this was done part by part. The warhead would be studied first by the artillery experts, and I would also be in these teams that, say, worked on warheads. Then also the propulsion, colleagues who work on gunpowder and other such materials, then also the fuse was studied by colleagues whose line of work that is, and so on. So all of this is done gradually to get to the final testing, and all of this with a view to economising, not squandering resources, not to fire I don't know how many projectiles in order to test something that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Andjelkovic Lukic during your period at the Military Technical Institute and in the course of your conversations and dealings with your colleagues at the Military Technical Institute, did you ever hear of the testing of modified air-bombs by that institute?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: I will tell you the following: In the reports compiled by Mr. Berko, my distinguished colleague, I found a reference to 50 bombs with fuel-air explosives in Pretis. There is one illogical thing that I have to draw your attention to here and that's the following: In the opinion of my colleague Berko this was 1991 or 1992 when they were made, and in his CV my colleague Berko says that in 1988, he talked to Mr. Zoran Maksimovic who worked in Vinca, and in 1989, he left his work on these fuel-air explosives because the experiments did not yield expected results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm -- my question is about the testing of modified air-bombs systems. I would like you to answer with a simple yes or no whether during your period at the Military Technical Institute and in the course of your conversations and dealings with your colleagues at the Military Technical Institute, did you ever hear of the testing of modified air-bombs by that institute? I need a verbal response, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, I did not, because it is certain that if I had heard about that or if that had been done, it certainly would have come to me for verification, or I would have been made aware of it. I never had that on my desk. That is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your preparation of the three reports to which you contributed and during the course of your duty at the Military Technical Institute, did you ever hear of the extensive and proper testing of modified air-bombs systems in Bosnia or anywhere in Serbia outside your institute?

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't have an answer to this question. I have not heard about this. I don't know anything about this, because from 1989 onwards I worked at the Technical Testing Centre and there was no mention of that. I really do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move, if I may, to the question of the ODAB. In your report, at paragraph 6.18, which is on page 64 of the original and page 72 in English. You say that during the war in Bosnia and Croatia, the Croatian Army possessed the Russian ODAB-500 fuel-air bomb and fired such a bomb from a MiG 21 towards forces of the ARSK, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MIRJANA ANDJELKOVIC LUKIC
